newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries higher on short covering before data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries higher on short covering before data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices were trading higher late Thursday amid optimism a budget accord could be reached and short covering ahead of a payrolls report.

The National Association of Purchasing Management reported its overall index declined slightly and initial jobless claims jumped 28,000 to give the market support in early dealings. Then talk of an imminent agreement on a balanced budget agreement propped the market up throughout the session.
The Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond was trading at 96-12/32 late Thursday, up 18/32 to yield 6.91 percent.

Also supporting the market was a coupon pass the Federal Reserve executed late in the morning to permanently add reserves to the banking system. Large tax receipts and a scarcity of paper have pressured the short end of the market in recent sessions.
"We saw choppy trading that was a bit positive due to early rumors of a budget deal. The coupon pass also helped the market," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.

Dennis said the wage component of the nonfarm payrolls report due on Friday may overshadow the overall headline number and the hours worked portion could be weaker due to a large amount of strike activity.

Dennis said the bond market probably could withstand a strong overall reading on jobs creation, for example 210,000. Economists polled by Reuters expected, on average, that payrolls would rise 211,000 in the April report.

She said the market seemed to be more preoccupied with the wage component of the report of late, and a rise of 0.3 percent likely would be viewed as neutral or slightly positive. A higher reading could undo most of the gains seen this week, Dennis said.
Limiting market movement in either direction were the refunding auctions next week as players tended to be cautious before going into a refunding, Dennis said.
"The news today on balance was very good. There's not much of a sign of higher inflation," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp.

Johnson said both supplier deliveries and the percentage of manufacturers paying higher prices were both down in the NAPM report and that was very encouraging as they were useful as leading indicators of inflation.

"They've given the bond market a bit of a lift, but not much will happen (with prices) until tomorrow's payrolls report," said Johnson. "Average hourly earnings will be very important -- perhaps as important as the headline number."

"I've been forecasting for three weeks now that jobs would grow by 140,000 based on the claims data. Unfortunately, the correlation between the claims data and payrolls is very weak," he said. However, the market was starting to build in an increase of less than 200,000, perhaps about 175,000, Johnson said.
A rise of 211,000 -- predicted by economists polled by Reuters -- could cause serious problems for the bond market, Johnson said. In fact, any number above 190,000 would be a problem, he said.
Trading volume continued on the high side, a factor seen pleasing to market bulls.
Prices were hitting session highs late in the session as players covered shorts ahead of Friday's payrolls data.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were down three basis points to 5.08 percent, six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.31 percent and year bill rates were down two basis points to 5.55 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 6.26 percent. Five-year notes were up 5/32 to 100-12/32, yielding 6.54 percent. Ten-year notes were up 11/32 to 97-even, yielding 6.67 percent.
